figures.label: Figure 1
figures.caption: OPAL (OPtimizer with an Agent in the Loop), our reactive optimizer, across different settings. In most settings without heavily tuned optimization hyperparameters, reactive optimizers improve the training loss and test performance upon the canonical choices. In modded-nanogpt, #2 is AdamW, #21 is Shampoo, #36 is a tuned Muon, and #30 and #46 are more elaborate Muon-based recipes.
figures.headline: OPAL matches or exceeds the canonical recipes in most settings without heavily tuned optimization hyperparameters.

figures.label: Figure 2
figures.caption: The two programs the agent writes and rewrites iteratively during training. With code as the entire interface, we give the agent maximal freedom to choose what to watch and what to change.
figures.headline: Two rewritable programs, updater.py and analysis.py, form a loop between training statistics and optimizer code.

figures.label: Figure 3
figures.caption: Training trajectories and code edits in four OPAL runs. Blue curves show OPAL’s loss alongside the corresponding fixed-recipe baselines; ticks below each curve mark decisions and distinguish code edits. The edit patterns differ across runs, reflecting module-specific changes made at different stages of training. The curves show the outcomes of the complete runs, rather than isolating the effect of each edit.
figures.headline: Edit patterns differ across four OPAL runs, with module-specific changes made at different stages of training.

figures.label: Figure 4
figures.caption: DeepSeek-V3’s learning rate, designed by hand (upper left), and learning rates OPAL set in four runs, as multiples of each recipe’s rate. The schedules vary across tasks and parameter groups and include mid-run rate increases as well as cooldowns. These are observed trajectories, rather than schedules specified before training.
figures.headline: OPAL's learning rates vary by parameter group and include mid-run increases, unlike DeepSeek-V3's hand-designed schedule.

figures.label: Figure 5
figures.caption: Changes of optimizer type and of precision in four OPAL runs. In some runs, the weights are simply moved to standard Muon, while in others, OPAL moves them gradually by module type and chooses high precision for a very small part of the weights, citing the signals it observed.
figures.headline: In four runs, OPAL moved some weights to Muon, sometimes gradually by module type, and kept a small share in high precision.

figures.label: Figure 6
figures.caption: A variant of the tilted double-well potential, one of the 34 landscapes we test optimizers on. The dashed line uses the blog’s static Preset A, while the blue line traces the reactive optimizer. The reactive optimizer raises its momentum along the gentle slope, lowers it as the gradient falls, and clears it when it overshoots, reaching the optimum where common optimizers at their default settings stall.
figures.headline: On a tilted double-well landscape, OPAL's momentum control crosses the flat stretch where default static settings stall.

figures.label: Figure 7
figures.caption: ResNet-18 on CIFAR-10 with four stretches of random images and labels, shaded. Left: test loss; markers indicate changes to OPAL’s safeguards. Right: the change in test accuracy in each stretch. Reactive agents can defend against the designed type of loss spikes, induced by data corruption, after seeing it a few times. Clean segments use Gaussian smoothing in log loss ($\sigma=300$ updates); the first 1,000 updates, corruption intervals and two evaluations after each interval remain unsmoothed.
figures.headline: With four corrupted stretches, OPAL's accuracy losses shrink after repeated exposure while clipped baselines lose 28 to 76 points each.

figures.label: Figure 8
figures.caption: ResNet-18 trained for 120 epochs on 45,000 CIFAR-10 images, 10% with a wrong label. At epochs 24 and 28, dev loss climbs and the agent reacts. OPAL counters the overfitting with progressively higher learning rates and a weight average it chooses on the development set. OPAL ends at a test loss of 0.685, compared with 2.493 for the final AdamW weights and 0.832 for its development-selected weight average; the test set is not used by the agent.
figures.headline: OPAL ends at test loss 0.685 on mislabeled data, against 2.493 for final AdamW weights and 0.832 for its weight average.

figures.label: Figure 9
figures.caption: Wall-clock time relative to the same task trained without an agent. Training that waits for the agent at every decision takes much longer (1.30× to 4.39×), while training that does not wait adds only a little time on top of the static run (1.01× to 1.14×). That remaining overhead is the cost of running what the agent wrote: an update rule that costs more per step than the recipe’s (such as Muon’s orthogonalization, or keeping a tensor in float32) and the measurement cost of its analysis program.
figures.headline: Waiting for the agent at every decision slows training 1.30× to 4.39×, while letting training continue adds 1.01× to 1.14×.

abstract: We study a reactive optimizer that uses a pretrained language-model agent to inspect training dynamics and rewrite executable optimizer code during a single training run. The agent can change update rules and schedules for individual parameter groups, without optimizer-specific meta-training or memory transferred from other runs. We evaluate this approach, OPAL, on language modeling and image generation when a recipe has not been tuned for the target setting. Across the evaluated settings, it matches or improves on selected fixed recipes. Analysis of its decisions shows changes to learning-rate schedules, optimizer structure, numerical precision, and momentum. Controlled experiments also show adaptation to repeated data corruption and reduced overfitting. We report these behaviors together with the agent’s computational cost and implementation requirements.

sections.body: The paper argues that optimizers are fixed before training, so they cannot react to loss spikes, stalls, or module-specific oscillations. It proposes OPAL, which uses a pretrained language-model agent to inspect a single run and rewrite executable optimizer code during training. The approach uses no optimizer-specific meta-training and no memory from other runs. The stated aim is to make optimization adapt to the training episode in which it runs. The introduction lists behaviors examined later: scheduling, suppressing loss spikes, and escaping overfitting.
sections.heading: Introduction
sections.headline: Fixed optimizer recipes cannot respond to training incidents, so the paper proposes an optimizer that rewrites itself during one run.

sections.body: OPAL is tested where no tuned recipe exists. Two variants of modded-nanogpt Track 3 (a 162M GPT on FineWeb) use Chinese, Thai, and Kyrgyz data, or a quarter of the batch size. OPAL is compared with five leaderboard recipes with natural adjustments, and matches or outperforms the best baseline in all these settings. On Goldfish, starting from the official recipe, Amharic ends at 81.11 against 83.48 bits per sentence on held-out FLORES-200 text (lower is better). A swept static recipe reaches 80.89; OPAL initialized from it reaches 80.73. On image generation, LightningDiT-XL/1 reaches FID-50K 1.83 against 2.18 with guidance, and RAEv2-B reaches 3.19 against 3.39.
sections.heading: Training without a recipe
sections.headline: Without tuned recipes, OPAL matches or beats the best baseline in every new setting tested, including Amharic at 81.11 against 83.48.

sections.body: The agent can rewrite two programs. updater.py holds the optimizer update rule applied at every step. analysis.py holds probes that extract training statistics for the agent to read at its next decision. Candidate statistics include the gradient norm of each parameter group, the size of an update relative to the weights it changes, the cosine between consecutive gradients, and tensors with unusually large gradient spikes. The authors chose code as the whole interface so the agent can change any part of the optimizer and choose what to observe. Together the two programs form a loop: training reaches the agent in the form it chooses, and its decisions reach each training step. The section gives no quantitative evaluation of this design.
sections.heading: Updating with spontaneous analysis
sections.headline: OPAL writes two programs: one rewrites the update code, and one chooses which training statistics to observe during the run.

sections.body: The section catalogues the edits made in four runs and in toy and corruption experiments. Learning-rate schedules were multi-stage, differed by parameter group, and sometimes rose mid-run; agents used A/B tests between two rates as evidence. Some agents moved weights from AdamW to Muon by module type. One kept the token embedding's Adam moments in float32 after measuring values about 15 in size, where adjacent bfloat16 values are 0.0625 apart. On 34 toy landscapes, the average log10(f − f*) score was −11.6, against −2.2 for the best of twelve common recipes. In the corruption experiment, the first two of four stretches cost OPAL 50 and 66 points of test accuracy, later stretches cost 12 and none, and clipped baselines lost 28 to 76 points each. In the overfitting experiment, OPAL reached test loss 0.69 and accuracy 78.6%, against 2.49 and 73.5% for final AdamW weights.
sections.heading: What is dynamically changing during optimization?
sections.headline: Logged decisions show OPAL changing learning-rate schedules, optimizer assignments, precision, momentum, clipping, and data gating during training.

sections.body: Waiting for the agent at every decision takes much longer in wall-clock time than the static run. The option to keep training while the agent reasons, applying edits later (a median of 65 updates later on Goldfish), adds only 1.01× to 1.14×. The LightningDiT agent made about 100 decisions in one run and cost USD 6.42 at list price, on top of about 74 H100-hours of training (about USD 510 at on-demand AWS price). Stated limits: the implementation does not yet support sharded training or optimizer compilation at larger scale; gains on modded-nanogpt are smaller because that recipe was heavily tuned and the run has only 3,250 updates; reactive behavior may reduce reproducibility; most experiments ran once, a few three times.
sections.heading: Real-world applicability
sections.headline: Letting training continue while the agent reasons adds 1.01× to 1.14× wall-clock time, and gains shrink on short, tuned runs.

sections.body: The conclusion states that optimizers have been written before training, and that an agent can keep deciding during a run. The authors say the mechanism is simple and general, wraps a standard optimizer, and assumes nothing about the model, data, or dynamics. They argue it is most useful where no recipe exists, such as for new scientific datasets, architectures, or languages, and that its gains over static optimizers are expected. The forward-looking claims are speculative: future agents might track curvature, use zeroth-order methods, or invent new schemes, and the section does not test these. The supporting evidence is the toy and scaled-up experiments reported earlier.
sections.heading: Conclusion
sections.headline: Most runs ended ahead of their starting recipes, and the authors argue reactive optimizers suit settings where no recipe exists.

sections.body: Appendix A places OPAL among related work on learned update rules, step-size controllers, population-based training, and reinforcement-learning optimizers. It states the distinction: OPAL adapts executable update code within the run, while prior methods already respond to training feedback. Appendix C describes the overfitting setting: a ResNet-18 trained on CIFAR-10 for 120 epochs without data augmentation, with 10% of the 50,000 training images held out as a development set and 10% of the rest given a wrong label. The agent did not see test performance. Logits are normalized with a centered LogitNorm to prevent loss-hacking. AdamW starts at learning rate 3e-3, also the reactive optimizer's starting recipe. Its final weights average epochs 96–117, chosen on the development set.
sections.heading: Appendix
sections.headline: Appendix lists related work on learned and adaptive optimizers, the overfitting setup, and decision records for the runs.
